name: Saratoga
place: Freeman's Farm and Bemis Heights, Stillwater, New York

events.title: Three columns
events.text: Burgoyne's army, about 7,000 men, moves south from its camp at Sword's House toward Gates on Bemis Heights, three miles off through thick woods. Fraser takes the right through the forest with the Advanced Corps and Breymann's Germans. Hamilton's brigade, with Burgoyne, takes the centre by a road over the Great Ravine. Riedesel and Phillips keep the left on the river road with the heavy guns and the boats. A morning fog hides both armies.

events.title: The signal gun
events.text: Riedesel records the signal gun at eleven. Hamilton's column crosses the Great Ravine by a small bridge and turns west for Freeman's farm. On the river road Riedesel's column halts beyond the Taylor house to rebuild bridges. Gates keeps most of his army in the works, wary of the column on the river road, and sends Morgan's riflemen and Dearborn's light infantry up the road from the Neilson farm.

events.title: Freeman's farm
events.text: The British picquets come out into Freeman's clearing, an old farm of stumps and weeds, and are shot down from the house and the fences by Morgan's riflemen. Almost every picquet officer is hit. The riflemen chase the survivors straight into Hamilton's main body, are fired on and scatter back into the woods.

events.title: Poor's regiments
events.text: Morgan rallies his men on the south edge of the clearing. Gates sends Cilley's and Scammell's New Hampshire regiments up to Morgan's left. Fraser's light infantry, on the high ground to the west, has its first brush with them. The firing dies down for a while about half past one.

events.title: Hamilton's line
events.text: About two o'clock the British regiments come out opposite the Freeman house: the 21st on the right, the 62nd in the centre, the 20th on the left, Jones's four guns between them and the 9th in reserve behind a ravine. One gun fires a shot through the empty house. Hale's New Hampshire, Van Cortlandt's and Livingston's New York regiments and the Connecticut militia come up one after another, stretching the American line west toward Fraser.

events.title: The action becomes general
events.text: By three every regiment in the centre is in action across the clearing, at close range, in smoke. The Americans fire from the edge of the woods. Wilkinson says no American general came onto the field until evening; the Park Service has Arnold directing the regiments as they arrived. Fraser holds his height on the right and is only partly engaged.

events.title: The clearing
events.text: For three hours the fight swings back and forth over the field. The 62nd charges into the woods four times and is shot back each time. The guns are taken and retaken; 36 of Jones's 48 gunners are hit and Jones is killed. Phillips brings four more guns across from the river road to steady the line. Breymann's grenadiers turn back an attempt to get round Fraser's right.

events.title: Riedesel marches
events.text: Riedesel hears the firing grow and asks Burgoyne for leave to help. He takes his own regiment, two companies of Rhetz and Pausch's two guns back over the ravine and about a mile and a half through the woods toward the sound. Toward evening Learned's brigade comes up on the American left and meets Fraser's light infantry and some Germans.

events.title: Riedesel strikes
events.text: About six, with the sun going down, the Brunswickers come out on the American right at the double with their drums beating. Pausch's guns fire grape into the woods. The Germans cross a muddy ditch, fire into the American flank and go in with the bayonet. The Americans give way.

events.title: Darkness
events.text: Firing ends about seven, when darkness separates the two sides, and the Americans go back to Bemis Heights. The British hold the field and lie on their arms all night in the cold. Burgoyne has lost about 600 men, the 62nd more than half its strength. Gates reports 65 killed, 218 wounded and 38 missing.

events.title: The fortified camp
events.text: Burgoyne forms to attack again in the fog of the 20th, then calls it off at Fraser's advice: the grenadiers are worn out. He entrenches where he stands. Fraser's corps builds a log and earth redoubt round Freeman's farm. The camp stretches east over the plateau to three redoubts on the bluff above the river, the Great Redoubt, guarding the hospital, the stores and the boats on the flats below.

events.title: Digging in
events.text: A bridge of boats goes across the Hudson below the Great Redoubt. For two weeks more than a thousand men a day cut trees for a field of fire in front of the British lines. The pickets face each other across the Middle Ravine by the Chatfield farm, and there are alarms and sniping every night.

events.title: Breymann's post
events.text: On a rise north-west of Freeman's farm Breymann's Germans build a wall of logs about 750 feet long, commanding the road into the rear of the British camp. Two stockaded cabins between it and the Balcarres works are given to two companies of Canadians. Militia keep coming in to Gates; Burgoyne's army shrinks.

events.title: Council of war
events.text: On 4 October Burgoyne cuts the rations and calls a council of war. No help has come from the south: Clinton takes the Highlands forts on the 6th, but the news never reaches Burgoyne. He decides on a reconnaissance in force against the American left.

events.title: The reconnaissance in force
events.text: At ten about 1,500 regulars, drawn from every regiment but the 47th, parade on the right of the camp with ten guns. Burgoyne, Phillips, Riedesel and Fraser all go with them. The light infantry and the 24th will take the right, about 300 Germans the centre and the grenadiers with most of the guns the left. The rest of the army stays in the lines.

events.title: Barber's wheatfield
events.text: About one the column moves off south-west and deploys across Barber's wheatfield above the Middle Ravine, a front of more than 1,000 yards with woods on both flanks. Foragers cut the wheat; officers climb onto a cabin roof with telescopes. Wilkinson rides forward to watch them. Gates tells him to order Morgan to begin. Morgan circles west through the woods for the height on the British right; Poor goes for their left.

events.title: Poor and the grenadiers
events.text: About three the British guns open. Poor's brigade comes up through the brush against the grenadiers, takes their fire and charges. The grenadiers break, rally and are overrun; every gun horse is killed and Cilley sits astride a captured 12-pounder. Acland and Williams of the artillery are taken. On the right Morgan's riflemen come in on the flank of the light infantry, and Dearborn's men fire, jump the fence and charge.

events.title: Fraser falls
events.text: Learned's brigade is thrown back by the Germans in the centre, then comes on again with Arnold at its head. The light infantry, called back by a misunderstanding, leaves the Germans open on both sides. Fraser rides along the line on a grey horse to rally it and is shot through the body; the shot was later credited to Timothy Murphy, a story Luzader thinks was invented in the nineteenth century. Ten Broeck's Albany militia come up behind Learned.

events.title: Back to the works
events.text: Wilkinson says the British line gave way 52 minutes after the first shot. Within the hour the survivors are back in the Balcarres Redoubt, leaving eight guns and more than 400 killed, wounded and taken. Lincoln brings Paterson's brigade and Putnam's two regiments out of the river works.

events.title: Arnold at the Balcarres Redoubt
events.text: Arnold takes Poor's men straight at the log and earth walls round Freeman's farm. The light infantry and the 24th fire over the parapet and Phillips's guns fire grape, and the attack is beaten off. Paterson's brigade comes into line in front of the works.

events.title: The Canadian cabins
events.text: Arnold rides north between the lines, under fire from both, to Learned's men, who drive the Canadians out of the cabins between the two redoubts. That opens the way round the south end and the rear of Breymann's works. Morgan, Dearborn and Putnam are in the woods in front of it, about 120 yards off.

events.title: Breymann's redoubt
events.text: A few minutes after sunset Putnam's Massachusetts men storm across the open field into the front of Breymann's works while Learned's come in at the south end and Arnold rides in at the rear. Within five minutes the Germans are overturned. Breymann is killed. Arnold's horse is killed under him and he is wounded in the leg. The Americans take the tents, the guns and the baggage, and the British right is open.

events.title: Night
events.text: Darkness ends the fighting. A German counter-attack under Lt. Col. von Speth loses its way in the dark and is captured. Burgoyne gives up the camp: the tents are struck, the guns and baggage taken down toward the river and the fires left burning. Before daybreak the army is round the Great Redoubt and the hospital flats.

events.title: The abandoned camp
events.text: The Americans march into the empty British camp and push riflemen up close to the Great Redoubt; they try to put a battery in and are shelled off. Fraser dies at the Taylor house: about eight by Baroness Riedesel's account, about eleven by Digby's. A sharpshooter's ball breaks General Lincoln's leg. At noon the 9th and the 47th set off north as the vanguard of the retreat.

events.title: Fraser's burial
events.text: As he asked, Fraser is buried in one of the redoubts on the bluff. Digby has it at sunset, Baroness Riedesel at six exactly. The chaplain reads the service under American cannon fire. Gates said later that he would not have fired had he known what it was.

events.title: The retreat
events.text: About nine, Burgoyne says, the army moves off north up the river road in heavy rain, Riedesel in the van and Phillips in the rear. More than 800 sick and wounded stay behind in the hospital with a letter to Gates. The pontoons of the bridge are taken up.

events.title: Saratoga
events.text: About four in the morning Digby's grenadiers, the rear guard, follow, breaking the bridges behind them. The army reaches Saratoga, off the map to the north, on the night of the 9th. On 17 October it marches out at ten and grounds its arms; at noon Burgoyne surrenders to Gates.

outcome.result: American victory: Burgoyne surrenders at Saratoga, 17 October
losses: Freeman's Farm: 65 killed, 218 wounded, 38 missing (Gates's return). Bemis Heights: about 150 killed and wounded, Arnold among the wounded.

Freeman's Farm: about 600 killed and wounded. Bemis Heights: over 600 killed, wounded and taken, with Fraser and Breymann dead and ten guns lost. The returns of 17 October counted 3,379 British and 2,202 Germans.
outcome.note: Burgoyne put his own loss on 19 September at 500 or more; the Park Service gives 590 and 630 for the two days. Gates's army had grown past 13,000 rank and file present by the surrender.

sources: John Burgoyne, A State of the Expedition from Canada, as laid before the House of Commons (London: J. Almon, 1780): his letter to Germain of 20 October 1777 and the testimony of Balcarres, Money, Harrington, Forbes, Bloomfield and Kingston.

William Digby, journal, in James Phinney Baxter, ed., The British Invasion from the North ... with the Journal of Lieut. William Digby (Albany: Joel Munsell's Sons, 1887), with Baroness Riedesel's account in the notes and the returns of 17 October 1777.
Max von Eelking, Memoirs, and Letters and Journals, of Major General Riedesel during his Residence in America, trans. William L. Stone, 2 vols. (Albany: Munsell, 1868), vol. 1.
James Wilkinson, Memoirs of My Own Times, vol. 1 (Philadelphia: Abraham Small, 1816). Gates's adjutant-general, hostile to Arnold.

John Luzader, Historic Structure Report: The Right Wing of the British Fortified Camp at Saratoga, Balcarres and Breymann Redoubts (Saratoga NHP, c.1973), quoting Hadden, Pausch, Uhlig, Milius, Riedesel's papers, Kingston, Rufus Putnam, Benjamin Warren and Dearborn.

Places: OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL), the NPS tour stops and memorials, US 4, Wilbur and Phillips Roads. Terrain: USGS 3DEP elevation at 23 m over a 7 km square, with the Hudson at its canal pool, about 25 m.

What is reconstructed: the line of the reconnaissance on 7 October (placed from the Park Service's descriptions, not the 1780 engraved plans, within about 250 m); the field outlines; Fraser's position and Riedesel's route on 19 September; the hours between recorded moments (the sources disagree by up to two hours on when the reconnaissance set out and when Poor attacked); the strength of every regiment, apportioned from brigade and column totals; the losses by regiment, split from each side's total for the day; the place of the American guns on 8 October; the arrival of Ten Broeck's militia; and the British camp line. The Middle and Great Ravines are taken to be Mill Creek and the Kroma Kill. Sunrise and sunset are set midway between 19 September and 7 October, which differ by about 25 minutes.
